p: Yeah, Council Member, I think it’s– we’re happy to have, you know, further discussions about that. I know it’s a model that exists here in the city and other offices that are PEG’d to a percentage of X budget etcetera. So, it’s something that we’re, you know, obviously happy to talk to you more about, happy to meet with you and talk more about that.

I look forward to that conversation, too. And then shifting gears, I know that our incredible Parks Chair will focus more on the details of this, too, but I’m representing the least– the district with the least amount of green space in all of New York City. Obviously the Parks budget is very, very important to me too. The challenge has been over the last four years. You know, we’ve been in a world where the Parks budget has not substantially or in any way really increase since we got the highest budget for parks four years ago. A lot of it relies on one-shots, and that’s as I always say, the Parks

budget is a workers budget, and the one-shots shouldn't be really funding core services, but really building on baseline services. So, how have you all– I know this is important to the mayor, too. How have you all thought about, you know, there wasn’t any increase within the Parks budget in the Preliminary Budget, but how can we increase that budget and move away from a world of one-shots for core positions like Rangers and things like that?

Absolutely. The Mayor has been very clear about his commitment to Parks, and clearly the advocates called for the one percent for Parks which we’ve looked at as certainly a goal that we want to get to, and we will make more investments in parks over, you know, over the course of our term for sure. But we’re looking at the Executive Budget to see the financial challenges that we have, what kinds of investments we can make in the Executive Budget as we move forward. It is a goal that we share to make sure the investments are there, and we just have to make sure we emerge from the fiscal challenges here, hopefully with the suite of options and state support and the enacted state

budget so we can start to make those investments towards that one percent goal.
HOpe to see us get there. Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you, Chair.
Thank you. Council Member Wong followed by Council Member Brooks-Powers.

Thank you, Chair. Thank you, Director. I understand the Mayor wants to– or he supports a rent freeze, but at the same time that in this budget I’m hearing the property tax increases, and I’m convinced that your increased property tax, the property owners will just pass these expenses to the tenants and small business, hence increasing the rent. It seems to be obvious, and then we cannot have any rent freeze if we want to keep raising the property taxes. Is that something you agree on, or?

The goal that we have is for property tax reform to provide the relief that we need from a system that is universally understood

to be unequal, to be opaque, to be regressive, and that is really where we’re focusing our efforts.

Okay. Director, I want to be very clear. New Yorkers simply cannot afford another tax, not a property tax increase, not an income tax increase, not a death tax, no new fees to park on their own streets, and enough is enough. At a time when the cost of living is already through the roof, government should not be reaching deeper into people’s pockets to solve a problem it created. This is not a revenue problem. It’s a spending problem. And my first question to you is that if the property tax increase or income tax changes and other proposals do not happen, what is the actual plan to close this budget gap?

So, our focus right now is working together really alongside the Council as well, to work with our state partners and make sure that the suite of options that were presented both on the revenue-raiser side, and also on the cuts and cost shift reversal side are– make their way into the enacted state budget. We are very, you know, appreciative of the assistance in the Governor’s

Executive Budget and in the legislatures One Houses already. That portends a solution, and so we want to make sure that we emerge from the state budget discussions on a more sound financial footing.
Has the OMB analyzed how property tax increases are passed through to rents, commercial leases and everyday costs?

The Advisory Commission on Property Tax Reform looked at this issue and they looked at– ad they referred to the fact that the incidents of the property tax on renters is difficult to pinpoint, but there is an understanding that leases, commercial leases especially that go to small businesses, do have that. And so there is some level of impact on renters that we have to look at as part of overall reform.
Okay. Do you believe that increases taxes make New York City more or less competitive?

We think that the suite of options that we put forth for revenue raisers including tax increases on the most

profitable corporations could help, for example, achieve in addition to state funding already committed. Universal childcare, for example, $1.2 billion was committed. We thank the governor and we thank the legislature for their commitment to child care and employees would be– would welcome universal child care to improve the talent pool here in the City of New York, improve the quality of life. To be able to draw on that talent pool for their corporation. So, that is– those are the proposals that we put forward, which we think could ensure to the benefit of all who have a vested interest in making sure that the city thrives.

Thank you. I have one minute left, so on more question. Does so-called rental payment on water bills is essentially a backdoor tax where money collected through the water and sewer bills is diverted to the city’s general fund instead of being used for the system people were paying for. Why– we reach out to the Water Board and the DEP, and their answer was to ask the OMB. So, my questions is why is OMB responsible for this policy

and who ultimately decides how much is taken from rater payers each year.

it is true that the rental payment is part of the revenue forecast, it has been for the past several years and it is– we are not– it is on impacting rates like. We don’t know what the direction correlation is with rates. We would like to allow the Water Authority to keep those rates at some point for the rental payment, rather, at some point. But right now it’s included in the revenue forecast, and at some point when we emerge on a more stable financial footing than that may change.
Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Chair
Thank you.
I have more for round two.
Round two, okay. We’ve been joined by Council Member Nurse and next we have Council Member Brooks-Powers followed by Council Member Riley.

Thank you, Chair and hello, Director Soliman. It’s a pleasure.

I’m going to try to race through my questions. So, I’m going to just ask them and I could repeat anything that you need me to. So, thanks to the strong advocacy from the Rockaway community. We have been able to secure $50 million in capital funding for the Far Rockaway Trauma Center. Does this administration commit to further advancing this project and committing additional capital dollars to the trauma center in fiscal year 27. In the administration’s Preliminary Budget for fiscal year 27 there are funding cuts to critical alternatives to incarceration and re-entry programs. Why is the administration deciding to cut this funding? Given the need to reduce the Rikers population ahead of the transition to borough-based jails, does the administration commit to increasing this funding in the Executive Budget? This administration has championed the need for more affordable transportation. One of New York City’s best tools to make transit more affordable is via the Fair Fares program. In this Preliminary Budget, the administration does not include any additional funding for Fair Fares. Can the administration

explain why Fair Fares program has not been expanded to the 150 percent poverty level today up to 200 percent of the federal poverty level and beyond? Excuse me, expanded from the 150 today up to the 200 percent and beyond. How much funding is this administration committing to affordable home ownership opportunities, and does the administration look to increase the funding in the coming fiscal years? My last two questions: This is regarding the insurance reimbursement state and federal issues. So, the federal Home Rule One bill includes several provisions that eliminate federal funding for specific Medicaid recipients. As a result of the bill, the Federal Government will no longer provide funding for certain groups of legally present non-citizens beginning on October 1st, 2026, nor will they provide funding for those who are unable to meet work requirements starting on January 1st, 2027. Approximately how many insurance reimbursement revenue do you anticipate Health + Hospital will lose when these federal cuts take effect? And assuming that the state will not be able to cover all lost funding for Medicaid recipients, what is the

administration’s plan to support Health + Hospitals to make up for the lost insurance reimbursement revenue for its patients who lose their Medicaid coverage? And again, I can repeat anything you need me to.

Thank you, Council Member. So, a couple of things, let’s take them in order. The Far Rockaway Trauma Center, is– so as you noted, there’s $50 million in capital that is there. There’s also $300,000 in expense. We know it’s critical to your community, and we want to make sure that we’re looking at as part of the Executive Budget ways that we may be able to go further than that. With respect to alternatives to incarceration, don’t believe that we cut that. What we’re just saying is that the Preliminary Budget is the opening salvo. We understand the connection and correlation with the effort on borough-based jails. And so we have to look at that with our respective agencies and see if that’s something as well we can fund in the Executive Budget. The affordable transit options, obviously Fair Fares– clearly this mayor has been very clear about making sure transit is affordable and

accessible. He’s talked about Fair, Fair, Fair Fares as a great legacy of the administration and Council working together to make sure the program is expanded. We’re looking at that. Obviously, the one time funding that was included at adopt, not the opening salvo and Prelim, but we’re looking at Fair Fares to be able to do that while at the same time pursuing fast and free buses. Homeownership, as well, obviously we want to do what we can to assist there. There’s a lot going on at the state level, as well, and look at what’s been included in the One House budgets, and so we’re hopeful that there’s also a state component to this where we can help on that. We believe it’s important that we’re helping, particularly first time homebuyers– be able to continue that. And then on HR1– so we’ve done a number of things on SNAP. like I said, not only SNAP eligibility specialists we added in the Preliminary Budget. We also tripled the food connection program at HRA at $54 million. On the Medicaid piece, we talked a little bit early in my QA session about the CMS and how they approved on the Elisia [sp?]-- is it Eliesa– the Elisia population to make sure that the

state isn’t supplanting with its general fund those costs. And that hopefully is going to lead to the no trickle down effect on H+H when it comes down to the impacts of HR1. So, we want to make sure Health + Hospitals is fully funded. They’re the, you know, first line for many New Yorkers on health care. So, we’ll continue to hopefully work with the state and make sure those impacts don’t trickle down to the city.
Thank you,Director, for your–
[interposing] Thank you.
direct responses. I really appreciate it. It was worth the wait. Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you. Council Member Riley followed by Council Member– Council Member Riley followed by Council Member– oh, he’s not here either. Okay. Council Member Riley? Sorry.

Good afternoon, Director. Your testimony you highlight significant

underbudgeting and the need to close fiscal gaps, but we also know that housing production is one of the most critical long-term cost drivers. So, how is OMB ensuring that the Department of City Planning is resourced both in staffing and capital planning to accelerate rezoning and land use actions that are happening right now within New York City?

Absolutely. So, we wholeheartedly concur with the goal on housing. I mean, housing just runs the gamut. Obviously, for DCP we funded a few things including sort of seed funding from the previous rezonings, etcetera. We also included some money there for some census work that they need to do. With respect to the housing plan writ large, we’re looking at the Executive Budget to see what investments we can make on the capital side. We have also created internally a couple of taskforces. We have the speed taskforce and we have the lift taskforce. So, looking at ways for public land so we can build on that, and also looking at ways to cut through the red tape and the bureaucracy so that we can get to, you know, buildings houses sooner and get to the supply side of the equation.

So, all those things are hope– are, you know, moving forward. We hope that we can get through the budget challenges so we can make those investments and create debt capacity room so we can make the investments in the housing capital plan.

Yeah. I’m really looking forward to the housing plan and what you guys come up with speed, but I also want to encourage you guys to look at DCP’s planners. DCP is losing a lot of their planners to the private sector due to the conversation that they’re getting. There’s a lot of borough offices that don’t have enough planners. I know in the Bronx I have a neighborhood planning– excuse me, a neighborhood plan, and currently right now my borough office doesn’t have enough neighborhood planners to help me out. So just want you guys to focus on that, because we do know DCP, a third of their funding does come from the federal government. So, want you guys just to put all of that in perspective. Because we know the Mayor’s goal is for affordability. We have to produce housing. We have to produce economic opportunities, but if we don’t have enough planners, if we don’t

have enough inspectors with DOB, you know, none of this really matters. It’s just policy on paper. Just want to put that out there. Another thing is you identify chronic underbudgeting in key areas. From a land use perspective, how has the underbudgeting affected the city’s ability to move development projects forward, particularly affordable housing projects that depend on predictable financing and timelines?

Yeah, so I think– and I’ll turn it over to Tara as well to add. But the less resources that you have to make those investments, not only in HPD teams that need to go through all the term sheets and go through the closings and all of that, that’s been highlighted time and time again. So we have to make sure that the housing apparatus is there to be able to do that. But it really runs the gamut. Anything on the expense side of the equation, if you have significant underbudgeting, you don't have the certainty, you don’t have the de-risking in the budget that you need to make sort of the long-term range approach and plan appropriately to get to the supply chain that you

need so that we can achieve our affordable housing goal. So, it absolutely has an impact. Tara– okay. I got it.
And we can talk more about it–
[interposing] Yeah, certainly.
later on. Would love to set up a follow-up meeting.
Certainly.

And for the last minute I have– we had a delegation meeting yesterday in the Bronx. Currently right now we’re experiencing a lot of fires, a lot of fires, and we sent a letter to request if the administration could help us out with including an extra firefighter in each firehouse or helping us with any capital repairs. So, just wanted to hear if we could get any commitment from you guys that you guys will actually look into this, because we haven't heard anything back from you guys as of yet.

Yeah, one of the things, I know that we have spoken to the union. The

union president had reached out and had spoken to me about it. Clearly it’s something that we need to see how we can have the, you know, best first response as possible in the Bronx. We know that there have been challenges there on response times as well. So, we’re looking at it. Clearly, this is a pilot that has existed, and we’re looking at making sure that we have the redundancy and capacity that’s there, and potentially expand the pilot. So it’s part of the ongoing discussion. We, again, have to see what the cost will be and how we can make that happen with the budget challenges that we have. But safety has to be paramount that is paramount. We want to make sure how we can close any gaps that might exist.
Thank you so much, Director.
Thank you.
Thank you, Chair.
Thank you. I think now’s a good time to pause for a five-10 minute break hopefully quick.
Sure.
Okay, because we want to make sure, and then we’ll come back five, ten minutes. So, please don’t go too far. Thank you.
Thank you. [break]
Excuse me, sir, in the balcony, thank you. Off the railing, please. Thank you.

Am I allowed to start? Can I start? Okay. Everyone ready? You guys are good? Okay. Alright, okay. So let’s resume with Council Member questions. And so next we have Council Member Restler followed by Council Member Morano.

Thank you so much, Chair Lee, for your wonderful leadership of this committee, and Speaker Menin, for your leadership. Director, it is good to see. I just want to say on the record, you’re one of the finest public servants I’ve ever worked with, and I am very grateful that you’re in this role. I am unbiased, but I want to congratulate on building a great leadership team. Originally a Staten Islander. Important to

note, but he moved out. The– I do want to highlight– just try and go through as many topics as I can, so I’m going to go fast, and appreciate brief answers if you don’t mind. What would be the real world implications if we were to fail to spend down the rainy day fund this fiscal year?

So, first, thank you. Good to see you, too. And the implications if we did not draw down what we had to do is we wouldn't have had a balanced budget for the first time in 45 years. We would have broken the streak if we put up a budget that wasn’t balanced. And we included as many tools as possible on the revenue side and on the expense side, and recognize thankfully the state assistance that was there. But at the end of the day, revenues have to equal expenses, and that’s how we balance. So that was where we ended out of necessity to fulfil our charter-mandated responsibility and our hope is the product from the state. When the state budget is concluded will allow us to see the picture in terms of how we can move to adopt it with a balanced budget.

Nobody wants to see the rainy day fund spent down or drawn down, but there’s no question we need to balance the budget. We need to maintain cash flow. We need to maintain the essential services that our constituents depend on. So, I’d like to shift to just some revenue generation and savings ideas. Firstly on parking meters– only 80,000 of the three million parking spaces in New York City have meters. That’s far fewer than the number of parking spaces on commercial corridors. That’s 2.5 percent of any street parking space in New York City has a meter. Do you support expanding metered parking to more commercial corridors across the City of New York? Has your team conducted an analysis with DOT of how many additional metered spots we could realistically add next year, how much revenue that could add? And if not, is that something that you could share with us by Exec?

It is, as I mentioned before, absolutely and important policy discussion that we are willing to have with all stakeholders. I mean, I think the fiercest competition is the competition for curb space, as we know, right? And

we need to rationalize our curb space policy working with DOT, working with all stakeholders whether it’s commercial loading zones and, you know, deliveries, and restaurants, and– right? So there’s so many– so much competition for space that we need to understand how curb space should be used as a strategy, and clearly there should be discussions about that which then could have also revenue implications. So, it’s an important policy discussion to have writ large.

Okay. We don’t– you know, it’s March 25th, so we just want to make sure that we’re having it in a timely way if this is an opportunity for us to help solve for some of the gap for next year while also supporting our small businesses because turnover on commercial corridors means more people are coming to shop at the businesses on our streets. Vacancy reductions, I went very hard at the previous mayor over the number of reductions that we saw during his administration. We saw that the number of actual city employees dropped to 280,000 during Eric Adams’ tenure, over 25,000 positions lower than the peak before COVID. And as Mayor Adams cut 10,000 budgeted, but unfilled

positions, on top of that from the city’s headcount. This has had significant impacts on the quality of services that we all depend on. We saw 40 percent reduction on the part-time staff of the Parks Department. We saw major increases in times to process cash assistance and other essential benefits at HRA. so, recognize there may be opportunities for additional efficiencies. For example, the DOC workforce where we’ve had high vacancy rates for a long period of time, but it has to be done with a scalpel. So I’m just trying to understand– and the announcement of the Preliminary Budget, you all announced that you were going to eliminate half of the vacant positions. Do we have a breakdown of where those positions are that have been eliminated? How can we get a better understanding of how that might impact services that our constituents depend on?

So, the scalpel is out. Scalpel is out and is being used. As is mentioned in the vacancy alignment exercise, yes, we said that we’re going to balance the equation. We’re going to say we’re going to reduce by 50 percent

vacancies with some exclusions, obviously, and then say that for the other 50 percent we're going to allow hiring up to a PS budget level by eliminating the two-for-one exercise. To your point, and you've heard very loud and clear from agencies on this, that there has been too many vacant position that have been remained open, that then affected city operations and city services, right? And part of that was from the constraint of the two-for-one, and part of that was just frankly sort of if there’s budgeted positions, we’re going to slow down, you know, the approvals and the pars [sic], and if it’s budgeted, we want you to hire and get up to meet what the operational goals and the mission of that particular agency. So, that is what we’re focused on. What we’ve seen, and this has been a build-up over years, there’s been a misalignment between the number of vacancies that have been there and the PS budget available and attached to those vacancies. That is what we’re looking at to rationalize it, understand where there is no PS budget, but we may need to invest, because those are critical operations. We don’t want to impact health and

safety. We want to make sure we’re not going to cut positions that are going to generate revenue because that just is a defeating purpose.
Sure.
We’re doing all of that in the approach. So, the scalpel is out, and we hope to have more updates on that soon.

Could I ask one more question, Chair– second round? One question very briefly. We have nearly 10,000 vacant NYCHA units and supportive housing units across the city of New York. We saw 12-fold increase in the vacant NYCHA units under Eric Adams. It was disgraceful. There’s over 6,100 vacant NYCHA units today. There’s over 1,000 of the supportive housing units that are in city control, controlled by HRA and DOHMH contracts. These are units that most– the people who most desperately need housing in New York City should be living in. Can we get a commitment to actually put a taskforce together to activate this housing and make sure that the people who desperately need it are able to move in next fiscal year?

Definitely something on our radar screen,Council Member. We have 144 million capital funding for upgrades and repairs between 26 and 28. There’s always more to do. In a previous question and answer session we talked about the 6,000 vacant NYCHA units. We want to make sure that they’re fixed so that we can make sure that we address the needs of those who are on the waiting list.

This is a management question and a resource question. There was no management in the previous administration that cared about this. We need leadership from City Hall and OMB, NYCHA, and HRA and DOHMH to actually activate every single one of these homes so that people who are otherwise homeless would have quality places to live. Thank you so much.
Thank you.
Thank you. Council Member Morano followed by Council Member Narcisse.

Thank you. Director, it’s always nice to see a native Staten Islander sitting at that table. Thank you for your

testimony. Your testimony makes clear that this underbudgeting was chronic and inherited, and I know Council Member Riley asked you a bit about the underbudgeting as well. Now that your office is responsible for the financial plan, why are we still seeing budgets that come in below known or highly-predictable expenses?

Well, Council Member, thank you. Always good to see a fellow Staten Islander, of course. We believe we’ve accounted for all of the known expenses that are there. There is an ebb and flow to the budget. There are needs that come up. For example, the budget– the blizzard that we had came after the Preliminary Budget was out. So, there are probably going to be increased snow costs that are there, something that we didn’t know, right, would happen. So, there are known expenses that we believe have accounted for with the addition of $14 billion in expenses which is unprecedented for the Preliminary Plan, and keep in mind, that was on top of the $4.7 billion existing gap for $18.7 billion, right, that was included in terms of expenses. So, we believe we’ve accounted for

everything, and to the extent that there are anything that exists that would be unknown, we’ll have to find a way to address those.

You’re proposing– assuming we don’t get the tax increase on income and corporate income taxes that we need from Albany, you’re proposing to close the gap in part through property tax increases. Can you break down how much of that burden will fall on outer borough homeowners, particularly Staten Island versus large commercial properties? Before you mentioned property tax reform which you know I support. I’d appreciate it if we could look at it in a pre-tax reform mindset.
So, I can’t talk about property tax reform?
Well, we can talk about it, but also answer the question as it is now.

Well, I think– look, I mean, I think on property tax reform just quickly– I certainly want to answer your question. The property tax reform proposal that we have under every model, every model that comes out, we know that Staten Island has among the highest effective tax rates,

right? So the one- to three-family homes in Staten Island under reform, those effective tax rates will improve. So, that’s just number one. Number two, with respect to the increase itself. We don’t move forward with the increase, just to be very clear. We did it out of necessity to fulfil the charter-mandated responsibility. I believe for an average one- to three-family home it would be a $700 increase per year. So, that is sort of what the impact will be. We don’t want that to be the impact. We do not want to strain the household budgets any further. So we’re looking– hopefully it would be a positive result in the enacted state budget so that we don’t have to consider the average tax rate increase.
You noted only four percent of new spending goes to actual programmatic needs. Does that mean 96 percent of this budget is just back-filling past under-estimates rather than improving services.

It goes towards programs that deliver important services to New Yorkers. So, it’s not to suggest that the 96 percent

is waste. It’s not. It goes towards making sure there are critical services like making sure that folks can be stably housed, like making sure the shelter system is operating, so on and so forth. So, the problem that we had with it was that we took a new approach. Budgeting plan by plan doesn’t serve anyone well, right? We need to make sure it’s out there. It’s reflected. It’s transparent and certainty and de-risking of the budget is important for all of us to determine what the resources are so we can plan to make priority investments, to understand what programs are rising, what units of appropriation are seeing that macro level, right? And we’re looking at a layered approach. Units of appropriation, budget code, object code, looking at KPIs and metrics, that’s what we need to do to see are they reaching New Yorkers in the most effective efficient way, and if they’re not we need to reinvest.
Can you walk us through the timeline of when OMB first determined the budget gap was materially larger than previously reported and when the council was informed of that?

I came into office– even before that, in my– at my appointment announcement there had been reports that were out there and there were questions that were asked about the fiscal monitor. The fiscal monitors are saying the gap is actually more than what it was reported, right? And so immediately the Mayor tasked me with doing an assessment. I met with this great team here and started to unpack everything in these major cost driver and understand so I can deliver an assessment to the mayor. The mayor, to his credit, as soon as he started to understand the extent of the under-budgeting, he felt compelled to publicly discuss that what we had said was the under-budgeting was in line with what the city and state comptrollers had said that the budget gaps were, and that’s why we were very open about that. Then, in the state budget hearing– so-called Tin Cup Day– we went there. We testified. After we started to aggressively look and manage what that budget gap would be if we put in the savings plan, if we took standard budget actions to reduce it, etcetera. That thing got us to the $7 billion when we went to the State Legislature and

testified before the joint fiscal committees. Then, next came the Preliminary Budget. The day before the Preliminary Budget, the governor committed $1.5 billion and there was an additional $100 million from a school aid run that gave us additional funds, right? So that is, what, February 17th. We came out with a Preliminary Budget. So, in a matter of a month and a half, basically, we assessed the problem. We were frank with New Yorkers about the problem, frank with the state legislature about the problem, and then we came to that gap that we had to close, $5.4 billion, in the Preliminary Budget. That gives you a general sense of the timeline.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Okay, great. Next we have Council Member Narcisse followed by Council Member Maloney.

Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Madam Speaker, and thank you, Mr. Director. We going to go– I’m not going to ask you those questions, but I want you to process it and think about. Last Monday, I have a child that got

killed, right, in our community in Sheepshead Bay, and previously we have more problem with that. I want to sit down with you to see what’s the plan, what can we do to make sure our children, our youth in our city not killing each. I know it’s a difficult one, but we have to come up with community centers. We have to make sure they have something. Idle hands, idle minds, you know what happen. It's the devil end I heard, but I’m not repeating that. Anyway, thank you. So, there’s a study with the State Comptroller Dinapoli [sp?]. Just revealed that New York City is now spending $81,000 per street homelessness person in a town where average take-home pay is about $40,000. And Mayor Mamdani want to spend more now, right? City Hall projected it will hit nearly $97,000. So, I will call it in the business world penny wise/dollar foolish, because we can home folks. Do we have to continue doing shelter, Mr. Director, based on the numbers?

So, Council Member, we are obli– we have a legal obligation to shelter the unhoused through the Callahan case. And so that is really what drives the shelter operation and the

shelter cost here in the city. At the same time we can focus on managing that operation to the best of our ability, but also focus on the affordability agenda. The mayor has been very, very clear about the need for more housing and affordability writ large through a multitude of different policies. And so that is really where the focus needs to be, housing supply and housing preservation.
Housing supplies.

Housing supply and housing preservation. And we need to manage the existing legal mandate and obligation to the best way we can working with our operational agencies to reduce shelter costs. And By the way–
[interposing] Too expensive.

shelter– well, yes. Well, you also want to make sure that city tax levy, that there’s a share that we have with the state. One of the things that we put out there were the cuts and cost shifts that existing in the One House budgets. It used to be for the single adult shelter

shelter population in the 1990s, it was a 50/50 split, right? State/city. It was capped in the 1990s and then was reduced further in the 2010s. So, $70 million that’s it, capped.
Okay.
For single adult.

Okay. Summer Rises, right now– in Summer Rises we serve over 100,000 students citywide with significant demands still unmet. How is OMB thinking about the long-term funding structure for this program, and if there is a plan to move it forward and more stable with current budget line?

We believe in what the program offers which is summer enrichment activities and programming for our youth. We have monies in the DOE budget that was added, $16 million in fiscal 26 to round out the cost there. So, we went from 90 to 106 in fiscal 27, and then the DYCD piece of it as well I think brings it up to about 146 or thereabouts. So, that is where we want to make sure that we’re investing in the program and we want it to be as effective as possible by drawing as many

And thank you, Chair. So, the Preliminary Plan included a $550 million reduction in the budget for labor reserve in fiscals 26 and 27. Over one-third of the total amount budget in the November Plan for these two years. This reduction was based on a re-estimate. This is not the first time we’ve seen a re-estimate. At last year’s budget adoption OMB also included a $375 million reduction in the labor reserve due to re-estimates. These re-estimates are different than changes that occur when contracts are subtle and funds are allocated to agency budgets for a wage

increases. The Mayor stated that the labor reserve has enough aside to pay for annual wage increases of 1.25 percent, starting in 2026, when the existing contracts begin to expire. Why was this such a large re-estimate in the labor reserve, and it has to do with the more accurate estimate of headcount? Would we not also assume that there would be savings related to the salaries of the over-budgeted headcount?

So, a couple of things on that Council Member. So, number of these savings that were taken in the Preliminary Budget are reflective of the way the labor reserved essentially works which is when there is a pattern established. In this case, let’s take the civilian pattern at 16 percent or the uniform pattern at 18.98 percent. Those reserve funds are put into the labor reserve to then pay for those contracts. We’re at about 98.-something settled contracts in the last round, and so the labor reserve has funding for also unsettled contracts that are there, right? Also, at the same time, monies that are parked in the labor reserve, according to the pattern to then be able to

fund those settled contracts. There are changes in,you know, actual experience. They could be headcount changes, etcetera, that then change and goes to savings that can be taken because they were initially budgeted, but data has changed, etcetera. Going forward for settled contracts, as you alluded to, yes, the Mayor said there’s one quarter percent that is in the labor reserve for future collective bargaining contracts. Where they will end up is obviously the subject for collectively bargaining. It’s a need that the City has to work on to understand that we could give a fair contract to our talented and dedicated public sector workforce.

There are also, you know, pay disparities for specific job titles that have been maintained and, you know, exacerbated over the year– years by pattern bargaining. And you know, historic structures that have solidified inequities that are often the legacy of gender and racial bias. This is particularly apparent in the cases of the paraprofessionals in the DOE and EMTs in the FDNY. Para professionals who work for the DOE both represented by UFT and DC37 continue to make

about $30,000 a year, and the pay– they’re– they play a crucial role in the public education system, and there’ll be an even higher demand as universal 2K and 3K are made a reality. And, you the DOE is really having a difficult time both retaining and, you know, hiring paraprofessionals to meet the need. And in the Fire Department, EMTs continue to make $18 an hour which is a fraction of what firefighters earn despite significant overlap in their roles, the high rate of medical 911 calls, and EMTs are also critial– are a critical part of the Mayor’s agenda for overhauling 911 response through B-HEARD and the Department of Community Safety. And you know, there is a– there’s a push to, you know, elevate those pay rates and, you know, the paraprofessionals are, you know, pushing for a $10,000 you know retention payment so they could stop the bleeding essentially. And just want to know where you are in terms of budgeting for these– uplifting these job titles and eliminating this pay disparity that we’ve seen.

Sure. We’re sensitive to the enquiry concerns. There have been other– there have been equity panels that have been

established to look at these types of things. I think that these types of issues are best preserved for the bargaining table, and also we understand there are significant costs as well that are associated with these. So, we have to figure out how we can balance that with the financial challenges that we face. But we are sensitive to the equity concerns that have been raised.
